definition.text: Using goods, services or natural resources faster than they can be replenished or reused.

facts.text: Applied to natural resources harmed by use, it means the same as overexploitation.
It is driven by consumerism, planned obsolescence, economic materialism and other unsustainable business models, and contrasts with sustainable consumption.
Long-term overconsumption in a region can shrink natural resources and degrade the environment.
Excessive consumption beyond the environment's long-term carrying capacity causes ecological overshoot, resource depletion and poorer ecosystem health.
In 2010 the International Resource Panel found household consumption for mobility, shelter, food and energy-using products causes most of the life-cycle impacts of consumption.
Growing economies can drive it: China's consumption surpassed the biocapacity of its natural resources by 1983.
Movements against it include anti-consumerism, degrowth, frugality, downshifting, simple living and minimalism, many aiming at a steady-state economy.
The term is controversial and lacks a single agreed definition.

definition.text: The argument that the richest consumers drive a disproportionate share of overconsumption and its environmental harm.

facts.text: A 2020 Oxfam-SEI report found the top 10% of earners cause over half of global carbon emissions, and the richest 1% emit more than double the poorest 50% combined.
The 2020 'Scientists' warning on affluence' linked growth-driven economies since World War II to rising inequality, resource use and environmental pressure.
Proposed responses include progressive taxes on high-carbon activities, curbing luxury emissions and moving priorities from GDP growth to sustainability.

definition.text: The state in which a species' population is larger than the carrying capacity of its environment.

facts.text: It can follow higher birth rates, lower death rates, less predation or large migrations, leaving animals competing for food, space and resources.
Judgements of overpopulation always mix facts and values; animals are often called overpopulated when they cause harm people care about.
In ecology the concept is used mainly in wildlife management, for example for the worldwide rise in deer numbers.
Predator–prey models of population cycles are also used to set the maximum sustainable yield of fisheries.
